A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Chain & Hash research. All 15 pages of v3 and 16 pages of v4, including their appendices, were readable. Text, equations, tables and rendered figures support comparison despite substantial reorganization.

before.justification: v3 reports original fingerprinting, model-utility, fine-tuning, quantization, LoRA and sensitivity experiments in Section 7 and the appendix.

after.justification: v4 retains original experimental results and reports additional benchmark, paraphrasing and comparator evaluations in Section 5 and Appendix A.

M1.justification: The hash construction, augmentation, KL anchoring and two-match verification remain. However, v3 Section 6.1 selects high-confidence token positions plus the next token for KL anchoring, whereas v4 Section 4.3.2 describes KL at each response position. The PDFs do not resolve whether this changes loss coverage or merely omits the earlier selection detail. The explicit combined-loss equation alone does not establish a new method.

E1.justification: v4 Table 1 adds IFEval instruction-following and GSM8K mathematical-reasoning evaluations alongside the four retained utility benchmarks. Section 5.4 also adds input- and output-paraphrasing scenarios, substantially broadening tested capabilities and adversarial conditions. Alpaca and ChatDoc coverage remains.

E2.justification: v4 Section 5.6 adds an evaluated comparison with Nasery et al. (2025) on Llama-3-8B-Instruct, including its default and use_chat_template configurations. The existing Xu et al. (2024) black-box comparison is retained.

E3.justification: v4 introduces GPT-4o paraphrasing procedures and a chat-template control for the new Nasery comparison. The stated adversarial meta-prompt count changes from ten to seven, although v3's plots already show seven named prompts; this does not establish scenario removal. Three-epoch Alpaca/ChatDoc fine-tuning, INT8 quantization and the required-trials criterion remain.

E4.justification: v4 Section 5.4 adds input/output paraphrasing attacks, with preservation and failure examples in Figure 4, directly testing previously unevaluated removal mechanisms. The six-meta-prompt and 100-question sensitivity analyses are retained in Section 6 and Appendix A.2.7, with additional explicit random-question results. Some earlier breakdowns, including v3 Figure 9's natural-question/no-meta-prompt Phi-3 ablation, disappear.

E5.justification: Three independently fingerprinted instances and averaging were already documented in v3; v4 does not establish an increase in runs. However, v3's separate Model 0/1/2 performance series are replaced by aggregate displays without dispersion estimates, reducing visible between-run variation. v4 Table 3 separately reports three runtime measurements.

E6.justification: Corresponding fine-tuning rows change substantially: natural-question Llama-3-Instruct/ChatDoc Pirate trials change from 117 to 1, and random-question base Alpaca+ChatDoc Weather trials from 304 to 6 (v3 Table 1; v4 Table 2). v4 adds benchmark, paraphrasing, comparator, runtime and verification-trial results, revises LoRA utility and leakage findings, and omits the Llama-2 LoRA plot. The causes of the revised values are not explained.

T1.justification: Beyond v3's informal security arguments, v4 Section 4.2 introduces a claimed 256^(-k) guessing bound extending to adaptive strategies. Section 4.4 adds binomial verification analysis yielding a false-positive rate of approximately 4.48e-5 under assumed match probabilities. Section 5.5 adds an N(N-1) fingerprint requirement for pairwise collusion protection. These substantially expand mathematical reasoning.

C1.justification: The two central contributions and LoRA applicability remain. v4's introduction adds an explicit greater-than-95% fingerprint-strength claim, and Section 4 explicitly asserts satisfaction of all five requirements. The earlier claim to the first comprehensive adversarial fingerprint-evaluation guidelines is dropped.

C2.justification: v4 adds explanations connecting non-fingerprint subject variations to harder brute-force discovery and IFEval gains to instruction exposure. It discusses paraphrasing costs and utility losses, plus Nasery's robustness-versus-instruction-following tradeoff. v3's explanation linking comparable LoRA performance to similar adapter sizes is removed; the constant-output limitation remains.

D1.justification: v4 documents Accelerate/DeepSpeed, the KL weight, non-fingerprint sample construction, complete evaluation meta-prompts, runtimes and a code-release link. Conversely, v3's tenfold sample duplication, 60-of-100 training meta-prompt sampling and explicit separation from evaluation prompts are no longer specified. These materially change reproducibility information without establishing corresponding training changes.

R1.justification: v4 adds Nasery et al. (2025) and positions Chain & Hash as an orthogonal layer that strengthens existing fingerprinting schemes. It also adds Hu, Cobbe and Zhou references for LoRA and the additional benchmarks, while dropping the earlier first-guidelines novelty claim. Most existing related-work discussion remains.

P1.justification: v4 merges requirements with the threat model, consolidates method sections, places question generation before chain construction, and reorganizes evaluation around the five requirements instead of model families. Discussion and appendices are extensively rewritten and reorganized. Author and conference-header information also changes.

P2.justification: The document changes from two columns to one, redraws the overview, and replaces many separate performance panels with consolidated tables and aggregate line/bar plots. Hyperparameter displays move to the appendix, new runtime/prompt/trial tables and paraphrasing examples appear, and some plots are removed. This is a substantial visual redesign.

improvement.justification: v4 strengthens evaluation coverage and documentation through new benchmarks, paraphrasing attacks, an additional comparator, exact prompts, runtimes and code-access information. However, Section 5.4 still claims random questions are more robust despite Table 2's natural-question advantage for ChatDoc-fine-tuned Instruct models. Section 5.3's stated natural-question average of 1.7 trials also conflicts with Table 5's approximately 2.43. These inconsistencies, unexplained result revisions and removal of training/test-prompt separation details and individual-run performance displays prevent a reliable judgment that the gains outweigh the losses in consistency and reproducibility.
